title: Probability in games
examples: How do I calculate the probability of rolling a specific number with two dice?
If I flip three coins, what is the total number of possible outcomes?
What makes a game fair in terms of probability?

explain.say: Today we are learning about probability in games. Probability helps us measure how likely something is to happen. We will look at dice, cards, and coins to see this in action.

items: Probability is the chance of an event.
It is shown as a fraction or a percentage.
It tells us how likely something is to happen.

explain.say: Let us start with dice. A standard die has six sides numbered one to six. The probability of rolling any single number is one over six.
Next we look at coins. A coin has two sides, usually heads and tails. The chance of getting heads or tails on a single flip is one over two.
Cards are another source of chance. A standard deck has fifty-two cards. The probability of drawing a specific suit, like spades, is one over four.
A game is considered fair when every outcome has an equal chance of happening. This means no outcome is favoured over another outcome.

draw.text: Fair Game: Equal chance for all outcomes

explain.say: Imagine you are flipping two coins. The possible outcomes are heads heads, heads tails, tails heads, and tails tails. Each has a one over four chance.

draw.text: Two Coins: HH, HT, TH, TT

faq.q: What does it mean for a game to be unfair?
faq.a: It means some outcomes are more likely than others. For example, if one side always wins, the game is unfair.
asks: How do I know if a game is rigged?

faq.q: If I roll two dice, what is the total number of outcomes?
faq.a: Since each die has six sides, you multiply six by six. There are thirty-six total possible combinations.
asks: How many combinations are there with two dice?
What is the sample space for two dice?

faq.a: Yes, you can add probabilities if the events cannot happen at the same time. For instance, rolling a two and rolling a three are separate events.
asks: Do I add or multiply probabilities?

faq.q: Is the probability of drawing a red card always one over four?
faq.a: No, there are two red suits, so the probability is two over four, which simplifies to one over two.
asks: What is the chance of red cards?
How many red cards are there?

faq.q: If I flip a coin many times, will it eventually be fair?
faq.a: The Law of Large Numbers suggests that as you repeat an experiment many times, the results will approach the expected probability.
asks: Does it take forever to be fair?

facts: A standard die has six equally likely outcomes.
The probability of an event is the number of favourable outcomes divided by the total number of outcomes.
A game is fair if all possible outcomes have an equal probability.
When flipping two coins, the possible outcomes are HH, HT, TH, and TT.

quiz.say: When flipping two coins, what is the probability of getting exactly one head?
quiz.why: The favourable outcomes are heads tails and tails heads. There are two such outcomes out of four total outcomes.

wrong.0: This is the chance of getting one head if you only flipped one coin.
wrong.1: This suggests that getting one head is certain, which is not true.
wrong.3: This is the chance of getting a specific combination like heads tails only.

quiz.say: If you draw one card from a standard deck, what is the probability of drawing a King?
quiz.why: There are four Kings in the deck, and there are fifty-two cards total. Four divided by fifty-two simplifies to one divided by thirteen.

wrong.0: While technically correct, the simplest form is preferred for probability answers.
wrong.1: This would be the chance of drawing a specific card, like the King of Hearts.
wrong.3: This incorrectly assumes there is only one King in the whole deck.

quiz.say: A game uses a six-sided die. If the game requires rolling an even number, what is the probability?
quiz.why: The even numbers are two, four, and six. There are three favourable outcomes out of six total outcomes, which is three divided by six.

wrong.0: This is the correct fraction, but the simplest form is usually expected.
wrong.1: This is the probability of rolling just one specific even number.
wrong.2: This is incorrect because there are three even numbers, not two.
